strengths: Compelling problem formulation: The paper identifies a significant and poorly understood drawback of existing cross-attention-based vision-language models—specifically, their substantial performance degradation on fine-grained, high-resolution document and chart understanding tasks compared to token-insertion models.

Simple, elegant, and effective design: Rather than introducing complicated auxiliary modules or multi-stage recurrent visual updates, CASA enables text queries to attend jointly to visual tokens and local text tokens. This naturally balances textual integrity and multimodal conditioning via softmax competition (implicit gating).

Comprehensive experimental validation and ablations: The authors evaluate CASA across two distinct paradigms—training from a text-only LLM backbone and adapting a frozen pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL). The ablations in Section 4.4 and Appendix A (such as masking text self-attention at inference, comparing directly against gated cross-attention under identical training budgets, and visualizing attention distributions) clearly support the core hypothesis.

Thorough efficiency profiling: The paper provides in-depth memory and latency benchmarks (Table 1, Table 11, Figure 5, Figure 6), demonstrating concrete computational advantages over full token insertion, particularly in long-context and streaming video captioning settings.
weaknesses: A noticeable performance gap to token insertion remains on fine-grained tasks: While CASA significantly outperforms prior cross-attention approaches such as mPLUG-Owl3, it still lags behind full token insertion on detail-heavy benchmarks (e.g., in Table 2, ChartQA drops from 81.6 to 73.4, and InfoVQA drops from 61.8 to 48.6).

Evaluation in the streaming video setting is somewhat narrow: The live video captioning evaluation primarily benchmarks against Q-Former compression variants and reported numbers from LiveCC, omitting direct empirical comparisons with other specialized streaming / KV-cache management approaches (e.g., StreamingVLM, Flash-VStream).

Analysis of window boundaries in complex multi-image contexts: CASA partitions interactions using image insertion points as window boundaries. The paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis or ablation regarding how window delimitation impacts performance when multiple interleaved images appear within a single prompt or across multi-turn reasoning steps.

strengths: Compelling motivation and diagnosis: The paper provides clear empirical insight into why standard cross-attention VLMs fail on fine-grained visual understanding (e.g., DocVQA, ChartQA), pinpointing the lack of concurrent text-to-text interaction and lack of implicit gating during visual fusion.

Simple yet effective architectural formulation: CASA cleanly reformulates visual fusion by allowing text queries to attend over both the relevant image tokens and local text tokens within a delimited window. It naturally avoids KV-cache inflation and expensive FFN passes for image tokens while remaining straightforward to implement via block-wise FlashAttention.

Broad and versatile empirical evaluation: The method is validated in two realistic regimes—training from scratch using a language-only backbone (Helium1-2B) and adapting an established pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B). It demonstrates strong improvements over prior cross-attention baselines (e.g., mPLUG-Owl3) across document understanding, OCR, general VQA, and video QA.

Insightful analysis and ablations: The ablation experiments in Table 8 (masking self-attention vs. text/image tokens) and the attention score visualizations in Figure 7 convincingly support the implicit gating hypothesis. Furthermore, real-world profiling (memory and latency in streaming video captioning) confirms the systems advantages of CASA over token insertion.
weaknesses: Remaining gap to full token insertion: While CASA substantially outperforms existing cross-attention baselines and narrows the gap, a non-negligible performance deficit against full token insertion remains on information-dense benchmarks (e.g., on InfoVQA, CASA achieves 48.6 vs. 61.8 for insertion on Helium-2B; 59.6 vs. 71.6 on Qwen2.5-VL).

Model scale exploration: The empirical results are restricted to 2B–3B parameter LLM backbones. Although comparison against mPLUG-Owl3 8B is provided, demonstrating whether CASA's advantage and training stability hold when scaling CASA itself to 7B+ backbones would strengthen the findings.

Contextualization with hybrid/sparse attention literature: Concatenating local text tokens with prefix/image key-values closely relates to windowed or block-sparse attention mechanisms used in long-context modeling. Discussing CASA's relationship to these general hybrid attention formulations would contextualize its novelty more precisely.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in vision-language models (VLMs): closing the persistent performance gap between efficient cross-attention fusion and costly token insertion, particularly on high-resolution and document/chart tasks.

The core idea—allowing text queries in the cross-attention layers to also attend to preceding local text tokens—is simple, elegant, and computationally sensible, providing an effective implicit gating mechanism without requiring bespoke architectural additions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering both de novo multimodal pretraining from a text LLM (Helium1-2B) and adapting an established, state-of-the-art pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), outperforming prior cross-attention baselines like mPLUG-Owl3 (even against its 8B variant).

Insightful ablations and analysis (e.g., Table 8 and Figure 7) isolating the mechanism behind the improvement, specifically demonstrating the critical role of self-attention within the CASA layer for regulating visual injection.

Clear practical demonstration of real-time streaming video captioning, highlighting how avoiding visual token insertion in the KV cache and FFNs overcomes memory and latency bottlenecks that plague standard insertion-based models.
weaknesses: A noticeable performance gap to full token insertion still remains (~5% to 7% on average, and up to ~12 points on InfoVQA), indicating that decoupling visual tokens from the global language stream still incurs some representational loss on dense information extraction tasks.

The primary experimental validation is centered on smaller backbones (2B–3B parameters); direct training and scaling to 7B+ LLMs would further substantiate whether the findings and relative advantages hold at larger scales.

Architectural variants such as CASA⊕ introduce non-trivial parameter overhead (~16–17% added attention parameters) and double the attention operations per block, which partially offsets latency gains unless utilizing the lighter CASA∨ variant (which exhibits a larger performance drop).

strengths: Systematic and clear conceptual framework: The paper deconstructs the architectural differences between cross-attention (CA) and token insertion (SA) into five concrete design dimensions (D1–D5), providing a clean and intuitive taxonomy that explains their respective compute/memory trade-offs.

Rigorous controlled evaluation: Unlike prior works where comparisons between CA and insertion architectures are confounded by differences in training data, scale, or recipe, this work provides strictly controlled comparisons (e.g., Helium1-2B trained from scratch and Qwen2.5-VL 3B adaptation on identical data).

Effective VLM adaptation strategy: Demonstrating that an existing, strong token-insertion VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) can be converted to cross-attention by training only the new CA layers and the final visual encoder blocks while retaining most of its capabilities is a practical and useful finding.

Compelling streaming video application: The live video captioning experiments convincingly demonstrate the practical utility of CA, showing near-constant memory and latency over long video horizons where token-insertion models rapidly exhaust memory or suffer severe latency degradation.
weaknesses: Substantial performance gap on fine-grained visual tasks: While the gap is narrow on general VQA benchmarks, CA exhibits significant degradation on dense visual/document reasoning tasks (e.g., InfographicVQA drops by nearly 20 points from 77.1 to 57.4 in Table 3). While acknowledged, this remains a key practical limitation of the CA paradigm.

Evaluation restricted to smaller model scales: The experiments are primarily conducted on 2B and 3B parameter models. Validating whether the observed trade-offs and adaptation dynamics transfer smoothly to 7B+ regimes would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Reliance on delimiter/gist tokens for video history: Operating with single-frame windows using only post-image delimiters as visual history achieves decent results, but the paper does not deeply analyze how much temporal context is lost over complex, long-horizon multi-hop reasoning tasks compared to keeping visual tokens.

strengths: Timely and impactful topic: As the vision-language community shifts toward long-context video and real-time streaming multimodal applications, revisiting cross-attention (CA) versus token-insertion is of high practical and scientific interest.

Rigorous and controlled experimental setup: Unlike prior comparisons across disparate pretraining datasets and recipes, the authors benchmark CA and token-insertion under strictly identical training mixtures and backbones (Helium1-2B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B), dispelling misconceptions about CA's inherent limitations.

Clear conceptual decomposition: The paper decomposes the transition from CA to token-insertion into five distinct design elements (D1–D5), offering valuable insights into which factors (such as FFN image updates and KV cache history) drive performance versus computational overhead.

Effective VLM adaptation strategy: Demonstrating that a strong pretrained token-insertion model (Qwen2.5-VL) can be converted to cross-attention by training only the CA layers and visual encoder blocks while freezing the LLM backbone provides an efficient recipe for edge and streaming adaptation.

Convincing real-world streaming evaluation: The experiments on live video captioning clearly illustrate the tangible latency and constant-memory benefits of CA over token-insertion and token-compression baselines.
weaknesses: Substantial remaining performance gap on dense reasoning tasks: While the overall average gap is narrowed, a pronounced deficit persists on visually complex, document-level benchmarks (e.g., in Table 3, InfographicVQA drops from 75.1% to 57.4% / 56.8%). A deeper qualitative or quantitative error analysis explaining why cross-attention struggles disproportionately with infographic and layout-heavy reasoning would strengthen the manuscript.

Exploration limited to small scale: The controlled experiments are conducted on 2B and 3B parameter models. Although training compute is substantial (64 H100s), verifying whether the observed trade-offs and the efficacy of parameter sharing hold at 7B–14B+ scales remains an open empirical question.

Limitations of the gist token history mechanism: For streaming video understanding, relying solely on delimiter 'gist tokens' to retain history inevitably discards fine visual details over extended horizons. While functional for general captioning, its limitations on fine-grained temporal needle-in-a-haystack tasks or complex multi-turn reasoning are not extensively probed.

strengths: The paper provides a timely, systematic, and well-motivated re-investigation of cross-attention (CA) versus token insertion (self-attention) for vision-language models, addressing the severe computational and KV cache bottlenecks of token insertion in streaming and multi-image settings.
The conceptual decomposition of the difference between cross-attention and token insertion into five concrete design dimensions (D1–D5) is clean, principled, and informative.

The experimental design is rigorous and controlled: by training both token-insertion and CA variants under identical data, compute, and backbone settings (Helium1-2B and adapted Qwen2.5-VL-3B), the authors convincingly show that vanilla CA performs significantly better than previously reported in the literature and that much of the reported gap was due to training pipeline differences.

The practical demonstration on live video captioning clearly showcases the real-world advantages of CA: achieving near-constant memory and latency over long video horizons, whereas token-insertion models rapidly exhaust GPU memory or suffer latency degradation.
The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and evaluates models across a comprehensive suite of diverse image and video understanding benchmarks.
weaknesses: A noticeable performance gap remains on fine-grained and dense visual reasoning tasks such as ChartQA and especially InfoVQA (e.g., dropping from 77.1% down to 57.4% on adapted Qwen2.5-VL), showing that cross-attention without token updates still struggles with complex document structures.

From an algorithmic standpoint, the architectural elements (cross-attention, windowed attention, gist tokens) are largely adaptations of existing concepts rather than fundamentally new fusion mechanisms; the primary contribution lies in empirical analysis and recipe validation.

The visual history compression mechanism across temporal windows relies opportunistically on existing chat template delimiter tokens as gist tokens; while effective, a deeper exploration or dedicated design for multi-frame state persistence is somewhat lacking.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small model scales (2B–3B parameters); validating whether these conclusions hold similarly at 7B+ scales under identical controlled training conditions would further strengthen the claims.
